solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Change around tempo for sometimes high instrument?

indicators.note: a word placed around another wraps it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: to change something is to alter it
the tempo of music is its time

explanation.surface: A musician speeds up or slows down a passage to suit some instrument that plays high notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tempo' and 'high instrument' set up a musical scene, but the instrument is a gauge, and 'sometimes' with the question mark hints it is only high when airborne.
explanation.definitionFit: This device measures height above sea level, so it is an instrument found high up in aircraft, though not always.

clue.text: Demonstrate removing mass for bridging structure

indicators.note: removing means taking something away, so a letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: to demonstrate is to march in protest
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: Protesters show the need for a bridge, minus the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: MARCH loses its M. 'Demonstrate' looks like a verb about showing, but it is a protest walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved span supporting a bridge or doorway is the classic structural element joining two supports.

clue.text: Student taking shower in slip-on garment

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a tee is a T-shirt, pulled on over the head
a shower is a brief spell of rain

explanation.surface: A student, still in a T-shirt, steps into the shower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' suggests a bathroom, but it is weather. The tee is split after its first letter to take in the rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone learning a trade or skill under instruction is a learner, much like a pupil or apprentice.

clue.text: Almost the ultimate check carpet

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: the ultimate check in chess is checkmate, shortened; the run of letters inside 'ultimate' is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A chess player nearly delivers the winning move, or perhaps someone nearly checks the carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' and 'carpet' look like verb and object; the chess phrase is one unit, and 'carpet' is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A small floor covering or rug is a piece of carpet laid on the floor.

clue.text: Slight disagreement limiting a king's list of duties

indicators.note: limiting something sets bounds on either side of it, so one piece fences another in

parts.note: a tiff is a minor quarrel
taken as written
R stands for Rex, Latin for king; the possessive belongs to the surface

explanation.surface: A minor squabble restricts the list of tasks a monarch must perform.
explanation.walkthrough: A king's duties sound like royal obligations, but the duties are taxes on imports.
explanation.definitionFit: A published schedule of customs charges or taxes on goods is a table of import duties.

clue.text: Broadcast rerun gets revived

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A TV channel shows a repeat that brings an old programme back to life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' and 'rerun' make a television scene, but the first word scatters the letters of the next two.
explanation.definitionFit: Rising again after a decline, gaining fresh strength or popularity, is to be brought back to life.

clue.text: Pub is empty after last one leaves

indicators.note: when the final one departs, the tail end of the word goes

parts.note: something empty is bare

explanation.surface: Closing time: the pub stands empty once the final drinker heads home.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'last one' sounds like the last customer, but it is the final letter of BARE.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking establishment serving alcohol is commonly called this, as is its serving counter.

clue.text: Brother to acknowledge prime minister

parts.note: Br is the standard abbreviation for brother, as in a religious title
to own up is to acknowledge or admit

explanation.surface: A sibling is told to recognise the head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown was British Prime Minister from 2007 to 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to a former UK head of government, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: Park keeper managed to get over bug mostly

indicators.note: mostly means all but a bit, so the final letter is dropped
in a down clue, one thing over another sits above it, fixing the order top to bottom

parts.note: to manage a business is to run it; past tense ran
a bug is an infection, or the germ causing it

explanation.surface: A park warden recovers from a minor illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get over bug' reads as recovering from illness, but 'over' just places one piece above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A warden who patrols and looks after a national park or forest is known by this title.

clue.text: Caught recent rattling noise

parts.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the latter of two is the more recent

explanation.surface: Someone was caught making a fresh racket.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket scoring, c means caught. 'Recent' for LATTER is loose: the latter is the later of two.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud series of sharp knocking sounds, as of pans or hooves, is a din of rattles.

clue.text: Promised a choice of three directions

parts.note: south, west and north, as compass letters
or is the word that offers a choice

explanation.surface: Someone was promised they could pick from three routes.
explanation.walkthrough: The choice word sits among the compass points, between west and north.
explanation.definitionFit: Having taken an oath means one has vowed or pledged solemnly, as in sworn testimony.

clue.text: Coldness trendy ahead of argument

indicators.note: going ahead means coming first, fixing which piece leads

parts.note: what is fashionable is in
a difference of opinion is a disagreement or quarrel

explanation.surface: A fashionable frostiness that comes before a row.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'difference' is a common euphemism for an argument, as in settling differences.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of interest, warmth or concern towards someone is emotional chilliness, a lack of feeling.

clue.text: Hospital home with tree given by former queen

parts.note: to be home is to be in
a fir is a coniferous tree
Mary was a queen of England, e.g. Mary I or Mary II

explanation.surface: A hospital housed in a building with a tree planted by an old queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Several English queens were called Mary, the commonest crossword queen after Anne and Victoria.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional British term for a medical institution caring for the sick, often in a town's name.

clue.text: Worker has loud complaint

parts.note: a worker bee is the standard crossword worker
f is forte, the musical direction for loud

explanation.surface: An employee makes a noisy grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud complaint' looks like one phrase, but 'loud' is the musical F and only 'complaint' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang, to have a grievance against someone is to have a gripe with them.

clue.text: Take a seat in which one may find rest

indicators.note: something one may find inside a phrase is sitting within its letters, ready to be spotted

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An invitation to sit down and relax.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a natural sentence about resting; the answer straddles three words: takE A SEat.
explanation.definitionFit: Freedom from effort or discomfort, a state of relaxation and comfort, matches repose.

clue.text: Bone in back and middle of rump

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, leaving off the ends

parts.note: the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: A bone located in the back and buttocks, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: The anatomical surface wants a bone of the back, but the bone defined is in the chest; 'back' is a ship's rear.
explanation.definitionFit: The breastbone is the flat bone at the front of the chest to which the ribs attach.

clue.text: Russian's ready to import British debris

indicators.note: to import is to bring in, so one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: the Russian currency, ready money, spelt the American way
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A Russian trader is prepared to bring in British scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective, but ready (or readies) is British slang for cash, so a Russian's ready is his currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Broken fragments of stone or brick left after demolition are the waste remains of a building.

clue.text: Archbishop, perhaps large chap under cape

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece lying beneath another follows it, setting their order

parts.note: C is the map abbreviation for cape
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
any man's name will do for chap

explanation.surface: A senior churchman, perhaps a big fellow wearing a cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape' suggests a vestment, fitting the churchman, but it is a headland. 'Perhaps' signals that an archbishop is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop is a senior member of the clergy, so he is an instance of a churchman.

clue.text: Consulted her about lingerie

indicators.note: turned about means moved round, so the letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone asked a woman's advice on what to wear underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of', but it signals rearranging the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Women's underwear and nightwear is a kind of garment worn beneath outer clothes.

clue.text: What dwarves do captured by wood elves

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the last letter of the first word and the first four of the second

explanation.surface: A fantasy scene: dwarves taken prisoner by forest elves, as in Tolkien.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tolkien flavour is the camouflage; the answer is in woOD ELVEs, and the dwarves of fantasy are miners.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwarves in folklore dig deep into mountains for gold and gems, so to dig is their trade.

clue.text: Tight chap is grabbing everything initially

indicators.note: grabbing something holds it in the grasp, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: initially signals the start, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A miserly fellow snatches whatever he can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' could mean drunk or snug, but here it is stingy with money.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is informal for stingy or miserly, unwilling to spend money, which is this sense.

clue.text: A block needs turning in light wood

indicators.note: turning round sends something back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a slab is a flat block of stone or wood

explanation.surface: A woodworker's block must be turned on a lathe in a light timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' suggests woodturning, fitting the scene, but it reverses the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This tropical timber is famously low in density, used for model aircraft and rafts.

clue.text: A Tale of Two Cities one's abandoned

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Roma, the Italian name for Rome, and Nice, the French city
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone has given up on reading Dickens's novel of London and Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dickens title is a red herring split down the middle: 'A Tale' defines and the two cities are ROMA and NICE, which loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval story of chivalry or a love story is a narrative, so a fictional account fits.

clue.text: Encountered yours truly on top of tram

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece sitting on another goes above it, setting the order

parts.note: yours truly is the setter referring to themself

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: The writer bumped into someone on the upper deck of a tram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of tram' sounds like a seat upstairs, but splits into a placing word and a first-letter pick.
explanation.definitionFit: To have come across or run into someone is the past tense of the verb meet.

clue.text: The day before is not entirely smooth

indicators.note: not entirely means falling short of the whole, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: a smooth surface is even

explanation.surface: Yesterday was a bit of a bumpy ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' could also give LEVEL, which hides the answer too, but EVEN shortened is the simpler reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The evening or day preceding a festival or event, as in Christmas or New Year's, carries this name.

clue.text: Chest many designed for sailors

indicators.note: something designed is newly planned and constructed, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sea chest built in quantity for people who go to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: A sea chest fits the sailing scene, but 'Chest many' is just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: People who sail yachts, usually for pleasure or racing, are a specific kind of mariner.
